# Introduction


Prostate carcinoma (PCa) is the second most prevalent form of cancer among men worldwide accounting for 29.4% of cancer cases and is the fifth leading cause of cancer deaths among men (Bray et al. 2024). In spite of this, PCa screening using prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing and digital rectal examination (DRE) shows no difference in prostate-cancer specific mortality between screening and control groups. Furthermore, there are significant harms due to screening including anxiety and bleeding as well as the risk of false-positives with over-diagnosis and over-treatment. Treatment of indolent disease that would have never developed into metastatic disease can cause considerable harms. Therefore, there is a need for both less-invasive and more-accurate screening methods to improve the effectiveness of early screening and to reduce the negative consequences for screening among men. Furthermore, screening methods should ideally identify individuals at elevated risk of aggressive, metastatic, or clinically-significant prostate cancer for early screening of prostate cancer via PSA and MRI to avoid over-diagnosis and over-treatment of indolent disease.

One approach to reduce the false positive rate for early screening and to reduce the risk of harms due to screening is to employ genetic testing to stratify individuals based on congenital cancer risk. The most common approach to genetic screening for cancer is with rare pathogenic variants (RPVs). For example, women carrying a pathogenic mutation in the BRCA2 gene have a 60% chance of developing breast cancer in their lifetime \[citation\]. There are a number of RPVs associated with increased risk of PCa that are, in some cases, associated with worse prognosis, including BRCA1, BRCA2, and HOXB13 G84E \[cite Tyler's paper\]. Carrying one of these variants can increase an individual's risk by a factor of 1-8.5 \[Tyler\]. However, these variants are at relatively low frequency in the population (typically, 0.05-0.10%) and therefore are of limited use in stratifying most people, though certain variants, such as HOXB13, are at a relatively high frequency in Scandinavian populations of 1.4% (Seibert).

An alternative approach to screening for RPVs is to use polygenic scores. In this case, many common genetic variants with small effect sizes are combined to calculate a score for an individual. Individuals with high (2-3x) or very high (3.5-9x) risk based on polygenic scores---comparable in magnitude to carrying a single RPV---make up as much as 20-25% of the population. Therefore, PGSs can potentially be more useful for identifying many more individuals at increased risk of cancer to target for further screening. Furthermore, screening for individuals using genotyping is much cheaper than alternatives such as whole-genome sequencing. \[One of the arguments for genotyping is that it is much cheaper than whole-genome sequencing, but if you are screening individuals for, for example, a BRCA2 mutation, you wouldn't WGS them, you would probably do a targeted sequencing panel, so I am not sure how strong of an argument that is.\]

Typical PGS models use case-control designs with logistic regression to calculate a polygenic risk score (PRS) to estimate the risk of developing cancer at any age. More recently, investigators have begun using information about age of diagnosis or age of onset in a survival modeling framework to estimate the risk of developing disease at an early age (cite Desikan). Genetic risk scores using this survival modeling framework are called polygenic hazard scores (PHS) and have been demonstrated to stratify individuals based on predicted age of onset for prostate cancer in multi-ethnic groups (city Seibert, Huynh-Le 2021). The most recent PHS for PCa has also been shown to be sensitive/specific enough to identify individuals at greater risk of metastatic/aggressive disease (Dornisch 2025). Furthermore, PHS can be combined with PSA screening and family history to potentially improve the positive predictive value of these screening measures (Seibert et al. 2018). By stratifying individuals using PHS, we can identify individuals who would benefit most from early PSA screening.

To date, few studies have tested published PHS models in populations that differ from the development set. One example of this was the PHS model of Alzheimer's disease from Desikan et al. (2017), which was tested in novel Nordic cohorts from Norway and Denmark (Motazedi 2023). While several PHS models for prostate cancer age-of-diagnosis have been published (Seibert, others), to our knowledge, none have been externally validated in populations that may have missing or imputed SNPs from the model. The earliest models in this area were criticized for being developed in European populations and for not being generalizable to non-European populations. However, more recent PCa PHS models have been developed in more diverse cohorts, such as the Million Veterans Program in the US, and have been shown to stratify individuals in multi-ethnic populations (Huynh-Le et al., 2021, Seibert, 2025 pre-print).

In this study, we evaluated the latest published PHS model for individual-level early diagnosis of PCa by performing external validation in two Norwegian populations. In addition, we performed whole-genome sequencing on a subset of individuals to identify RPVs and compare the efficacy of screening using PHS and RPVs. Lastly, we validated whether the PHS601 model is sensitive enough to identify individuals at increased risk of metastatic disease. Norway offers a unique opportunity for investigating these questions due to their well-developed electronic health records system, which allows investigators to link patient data from disparate health registries including the cancer registry and the death registry.

# Methods

## Subjects/Study Population

Two Norwegian cohorts were included in this study. The first we will refer to as the Norwegian Familial Cancer Study (NFCS). Subjects in this cohort were recruited in 1980-1995 from all of Norway via self-report based on over-representation of cancer in their families. Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood samples using the DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit (Qiagen, Germantown, MD, USA), following the manufacturer’s protocol, and analyzed using the Illumina OmniExpress 24 v1.1 chip at deCODE genetics (Reykjavik, Iceland) \[cite Mattingsdal\]. The genotyped dataset consisted of 15,769 subjects with 713,014 SNPs. Genotype data were imputed using a reference panel from The Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort (MoBa) with the MoBa pipeline \[cite Corfield et al. I guess\]. After imputation, the dataset consisted of 7,526,252 SNPs. 

The second cohort was the Hordaland Health Studies (Helseundersøkelsene i Hordaland) (HUSK). This cohort was recruited from Rogaland county in western Norway in two waves. The fist wave was in 1992/1993 and the second wave was in 1997/1999.  \[How was HUSK genotyping and imputation performed?\] Imputation was performed again using the MoBa pipeline with the 

Prior to analysis, each dataset was filtered to remove female subjects, subjects under age 40, and subjects lacking genotype data. 

## Characterization of PCa Cases

Prostate cancer cases were defined as male subjects with ICD10 code C61. Diagnosis date was the fist instance of this ICD10 code in the registry data. Controls were censored at age of last observation. Metastatic disease was defined as disease prevalence at the time of diagnosis that extends to lymph nodes inside or outside the same body region, organ metastasis outside the body region, and microscopic or macroscopic ingrowth into neighboring structures. 


## Clean summary statistics and PHS calculation

```{r css-summary}
css_summary = read_tsv(here("data/results/p212_PHS601_css_summary.tsv"))
``` 

We evaluated the performance of the PCa PHS model PHS601 (cite). Summary statistics from this model were acquired by contacting the authors. The summary statistics file was pre-processed with the cleansumstats pipeline to harmonize effect and reference alleles as well as chromosome positions and RSIDs with revision 37 of the 1KG reference panel \[reference?\]. This pipeline removed palindromes, indels, and impossible allele pairs and removed SNPs from the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) (cite this). The reference panel for our imputation did not include indels so their removal would not affect the results. Both summary statistics for the model and genotype data for the subjects were processed through cleansumstats. After the pipeline, of the initial 601 SNPs in PHS601, `r css_summary$removed_css` SNPs were removed as palindromes (i.e., ambiguous allele pairs), indels, or impossible allele pairs leaving `r css_summary$post_snps` SNPs in the model. In addition, the genotype files from the two cohorts were processed through the cleansumstats pipeline to insure that RSIDs and effect alleles matched between the model and the genotype data. Of the `r css_summary$post_snps` SNPs remaining from PHS601, `r css_summary$missing_geno` SNPs were missing from the NFCS genotype data, which meant the PHSes for these subjects were calculated from the remaining `r css_summary$end_snps` SNPs. Likewise, ## SNPs were missing from the HUSK genotype data so the PHSes for these SNPs were calculated from ## SNPs remaining from PHS601. Polygenic hazard scores were calculated for each cohort via matrix multiplication. The resulting PHSes were centered and scaled prior to modeling.

## Sequencing and variant calling

Information on number of subjects with wgs, sequencing platform, QC, etc. 

Variant calling was performed using the CPSR package \[Nakken et al. 2021\]. We identified individuals with 1 or 2 copies of pathogenic variants known to be associated with incrased risk of PCa including mutations within the genes ATM, BRCA1, BRCA2, HOXB13, MLH1, MLH2, and MSH6.

## Statistics

Polygenic hazard scores were evaluated in both cohorts using Cox proportional hazards models using the `coxph` function from the `survival` package in `R` (cite). For the any-PCa model, events were defined as age of first PCa diagnosis and controls were censored at age of last observation. For the metastatic PCa model, events were defined as age at first metastatic disease diagnosis. Polygenic hazard scores were centered and scaled prior to model fit. After model fitting, subjects were separated by centile range of PHS into the top 20%, the bottom 20%, and the middle 60% for plotting of K-M curves. Performance of each model is reported as HR~SD~, which is the hazard ratio increase for a 1 standard deviation increase in PHS, HR~80/20~, which is the hazard ratio between the top 20% and the bottom 20% of PHS, HR~80/50~, which is the hazard ratio between the top 20% and the median PHS, as well as the C index. For these metrics, confidence intervals were generated using 999 bootstrap iterations.

The effect of RPVs was evaluted only in the NFCS cohort. To test whether RPVs were at higher frequency in cases than in controls, we used the one-sided Fisher's exact test. Two genes for which no variants were observed in our cohort (MSH2 and MSH6) were removed prior to analysis. The remaining 5 genes were tested individually as well as aggregated as individuals carrying any of the variants. The p-values from these tests were adjusted using the Benjamini & Hochberg correction (1995). The one gene at elevated frequency in the cases (HOXb13) was then used in a Cox survival analysis to estimate the risk of PCa associated with carrying this pathogenic variants. This model was evaluated based on the HR between carriers and non-carriers as well as the C index. To test whether individuals with high PHS were more likely to carry a rare variant, we used logistic regression. To compare the HOXB13 carriers to PHS, we subsetted the dataset for individuals with both WGS and genotyping and refit the Cox model of PHS with this smaller sample and calculated the HR for a similar proportion of individuals as were HOXB13 carriers. In this case, 1.7% of subjects carried a HOXB13 mutation so we calculated the HR between the top 1.7% of PHSes and the median subject.  

All Cox models were evaluated for the proportional hazards assumption using the `cox.zph` and by inspecting plots of the Schoenfeld residuals versus time via `plot.cox.zph` (Cite Grambsch and Therneau 1994 Biometrika). Coefficients that violated the proportionality assumption were refit with time-dependendent covariates. In each case, the decline in HR was roughly linear so we used a linear time transform (i.e., PHS $\cdot$ age) for the time-dependent PHS with the `tt` function.

## PHS601 accurately stratifies Norwegian cohorts based on PCa risk

We first tested the performance of PHS601 in stratifying any PCa diagnosis in two Norwegian cohorts. In the HUSK cohort, there were `{r} p2521_sample_size[1, 3]` individuals with a PCa diagnosis and `{r} format(p2521_sample_size[[1, 4]], scientific = FALSE)` controls. The Cox proportional hazards model showed a `r (round(p2521_PHS601[1, 3], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk of PCa for a 1 standard deviation increase in PHS (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601[1, "value"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601[1, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601[1, "conf.high"], 2))`]; @{tbl-1}). Individuals with PHS in the top quintile had over `{r} floor(p2521_PHS601[2, 3])` times greater risk of any PCa than individuals in the bottom quintile (HR~80/20~: `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601[2, 3], 2))`, 95\% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601[2, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601[2, 5], 2))`\]) and `{r} (round(p2521_PHS601[4, 3], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk than the median individual (HR~80/50~: `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601[4, 3], 2))`, 95\% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601[4, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601[4, 5], 2))`\]; @{fig-phs}A).

The proportionality test and plot of weighted residuals revealed a negative trend in HR with age suggesting that the proportionality assumption was invalid for PHS (Chi. sq. = `r round(p2521_zph[1, "chisq"], 2)`, df = `r p2521_zph[1, "df"]`, p = `r pvalr(p2521_zph[1, "p"])`). The effect size seemed to decrease roughly linearly with age so we refit the model as an extended Cox model with a time-dependent PHS covariate with a linear time transform and a y-intercept at age 40. In this model, there was an `r p2521_coxph_results %>% filter(model == "phs_tt" & term == "phs") %>% pull(estimate) %>% round(2) * 100 - 100`\% increase in risk for a 1 standard deviation increase in PHS at age 40 (HR = `r p2521_coxph_results %>% filter(model == "phs_tt" & term == "phs") %>% pull(estimate) %>% sprintf("%.2f", .)`, 95% CI [`r p2521_coxph_results %>% filter(model == "phs_tt" & term == "phs") %>% pull(conf.low) %>% round(2) %>% sprintf("%.2f", .)`, `r p2521_coxph_results %>% filter(model == "phs_tt" & term == "phs") %>% pull(conf.high) %>% round(2) %>% sprintf("%.2f", .)`], p `r p2521_coxph_results %>% filter(model == "phs_tt" & term == "phs") %>% pull(p.value) %>% pvalr()`), which declined by `r round(1 - p2521_coxph_results[4, "estimate"], 3) * 100`\% per year (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[4, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[4, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[4, "conf.high"], 2))`], p = `{r} pvalr(p2521_coxph_results[4, "p.value"])`). However, the time varying effect size was weak and the weighted residual plot showed a wide spread demonstrating high variability in the time-varying coefficient. Therefore, in the previous paragraph and in @{fig-phs}A we have presented the Cox model without the time-transformed PHS.

In the NFCS cohort, there were `{r} p212_sample_size[1, 3]` individuals with a PCa diagnosis and `{r} p212_sample_size[1, 4]` controls. The Cox proportional hazards model showed an `r (round(p212_PHS601[1, 3], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk of PCa for a 1 standard deviation increase in PHS (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601[1, "value"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601[1, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601[1, "conf.high"], 2))`]; @{tbl-1}). Individuals with PHS in the top quintile had over `{r} floor(p212_PHS601[2, 3])` times greater risk of any PCa than individuals in the bottom quintile (HR~80/20~: `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601[2, 3], 2))`, 95\% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601[2, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601[2, 5], 2))`\]) and `{r} (round(p212_PHS601[4, 3], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk than the median individual (HR~80/50~: `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601[4, 3], 2))`, 95\% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601[4, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601[4, 5], 2))`\]; @{fig-phs}B).

Similar to the HUSK cohort, in the NFCS cohort, the proportionality test and plot of weighted residuals revealed a negative trend in HR with age (Chi. sq. = `r round(p212_zph[1, "chisq"], 2)`, df = `r p212_zph[1, "df"]`, p = `r pvalr(p212_zph[1, "p"])`). We again fit the model as an extended Cox model with a time-dependent PHS covariate with a linear time transform and a y-intercept at age 40. In this model, there was a `r p212_coxph_results %>% filter(model == "phs_tt" & term == "phs") %>% pull(estimate) %>% round(2) * 100 - 100`\% increase in risk for a 1 standard deviation increase in PHS at age 40 (HR = `r p212_coxph_results %>% filter(model == "phs_tt" & term == "phs") %>% pull(estimate) %>% sprintf("%.2f", .)`, 95% CI [`r p212_coxph_results %>% filter(model == "phs_tt" & term == "phs") %>% pull(conf.low) %>% round(2) %>% sprintf("%.2f", .)`, `r p212_coxph_results %>% filter(model == "phs_tt" & term == "phs") %>% pull(conf.high) %>% round(2) %>% sprintf("%.2f", .)`], p `r p212_coxph_results %>% filter(model == "phs_tt" & term == "phs") %>% pull(p.value) %>% pvalr()`), which declined by `r round(1 - p212_coxph_results[4, "estimate"], 3) * 100`\% per year (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[4, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[4, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[4, "conf.high"], 2))`], p = `{r} pvalr(p212_coxph_results[4, "p.value"])`). However, the time varying effect size was weak and the weighted residual plot showed a wide spread demonstrating high variability in the time-varying coefficient. Therefore, in the previous paragraph and in @{fig-phs}B we have presented the Cox model without the time-transformed PHS.

## PHS601 demonstrates specificity for metastatic PCa in Norwegian cohorts

In addition to evaluating the performance of PHS601 in stratifying individuals based on risk of any PCa, we were also interested in the specificity of PHS601 for aggressive disease. In the HUSK cohort, `{r} p2521_sample_size[2, 3]` individuals had been diagnosed with metastatic disease leaving `{r} format(p2521_sample_size[[2, 4]], scientific = FALSE)` controls. The Cox proportional hazards model of metastatic disease showed a `{r} (round(p2521_PHS601_meta[1, "value"], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk of metastatic disease for a 1 standard deviation increase in PHS (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601_meta[1, "value"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601_meta[1, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601_meta[1, "conf.high"], 2))`]; @{tbl-1}). Individuals with PHS in the top quintile had over `{r} floor(p2521_PHS601_meta[2, 3])` times greater risk of metastatic disease than individuals in the bottom quintile (HR~80/20~: `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601_meta[2, 3], 2))`, 95% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601_meta[2, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601_meta[2, 5], 2))`\]) and `{r} (round(p2521_PHS601_meta[4, 3], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk than the median individual (HR~80/50~: `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601_meta[4, 3], 2))`, 95% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601_meta[4, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601_meta[4, 5], 2))`\]; @{fig-meta}A)

In the NFCS cohort, `{r} p212_sample_size[2, 3]` individuals had been diagnosed with metastatic disease leaving `{r} p212_sample_size[2, 4]` controls. The Cox proportional hazards model of metastatic disease showed a `{r} (round(p212_PHS601_meta[1, "value"], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk of metastatic disease for a 1 standard deviation increase in PHS (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601_meta[1, "value"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601_meta[1, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601_meta[1, "conf.high"], 2))`]; @{tbl-1}). Individuals with PHS in the top quintile had over `{r} floor(p212_PHS601_meta[2, 3])` times greater risk of metastatic disease than individuals in the bottom quintile (HR~80/20~: `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601_meta[2, 3], 2))`, 95% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601_meta[2, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601_meta[2, 5], 2))`\]) and `{r} (round(p212_PHS601_meta[4, 3], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk than the median individual (HR~80/50~: `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601_meta[4, 3], 2))`, 95% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601_meta[4, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601_meta[4, 5], 2))`\]; @{fig-meta}B)

## PHS and HOXB13 independently contribute to increased PCa risk in the NFCS cohort

We next compared the performance of RPVs and PHSes in predicting any PCa. Only the NFCS cohort received whole-genome sequencing so the HUSK cohort was excluded from these analyses. We first subsetted our dataset to include only subjects that received both whole genome sequencing and genotyping. We then re-analyzed the PHS data on this smaller subsample to compare it to the performance of the rare pathogenic variants. There were a total of `{r} wgs_summary[2]` subjects with whole-genome sequencing of which `{r} wgs_summary[1]` were cases and `{r} wgs_summary[2] - wgs_summary[1]` were controls. Among these individuals, a total of `{r} wgs_summary[10]` had a deleterious mutation in one of the seven genes that we investigated: BRCA1, BRCA2, HOXB13, MLH1, ATM, MSH2, and MSH6. No subjects were observed with mutations in MSH2 or MSH6 so these genes were removed from the analysis.

As a preliminary analysis, we tested whether the frequency of mutations was greater in cases than in controls for each gene using a one-sided Fisher's exact test. Only the HOXB13 gene showed increased frequency in the cases than in the controls (OR = `r sprintf("%.2f", round(fisher[2, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% lower confidence bound = `r sprintf("%.2f", round(fisher[2, "conf.low"], 2))`, adj. p = `{r} pvalr(fisher[2, "p.adjust"], digits = 2)`). Therefore, we only proceeded with testing the risk of diagnosis with this gene. The HOXB13 gene mutation was at a frequency of `r round(wgs_summary$hoxb13_carrier_1 / wgs_summary$wgs_1 * 100, 1)`\% in the WGS subsample and having a high polygenic score did not appear to be associated with being more likely to carry a rare variant (OR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(binomial_phs_hoxb13[2, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(binomial_phs_hoxb13[2, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(binomial_phs_hoxb13[2, "conf.high"], 2))`], p = `{r} pvalr(binomial_phs_hoxb13[[2, "p.value"]])`).

Using the subsetted WGS sample, the Cox proportional hazards model for PHS showed an `{r} (round(wgs_phs[1, "value"], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk of PCa for a 1 standard deviation increase in PHS (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs[1, "value"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs[1, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs[1, "conf.high"], 2))`]). Individuals with PHS in the top quintile had over `{r} floor(wgs_phs[2, 3])` times greater risk of any PCa than individuals in the bottom quintile (HR~80/20~: `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs[2, 3], 2))`, 95\% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs[2, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs[2, 5], 2))`\]) and `{r} (round(wgs_phs[4, 3], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk than the median individual (HR~80/50~: `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs[4, 3], 2))`, 95\% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs[4, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs[4, 5], 2))`\]; @{fig-hoxb13}A). By comparison, the Cox proportional hazards model for HOXB13 carriers showed a `{r} round(wgs_hoxb13[1, "value"], 1)` times greater risk of PCa for carriers of HOXB13 mutations than non-carriers (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_hoxb13[1, "value"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_hoxb13[1, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_hoxb13[1, "conf.high"], 2))`]; @{fig-hoxb13}B). 

Combining these two predictors into a single Cox model, we found that both PHS and HOXB13 carrier status can independently contribute to increased PCa risk. In the combined main effect model, a 1 standard deviation increase in PHS led to a `{r} (round(wgs_results[3, 2], 2) * 100) - 100`\% increase PCa risk (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[3, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[3, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[3, "conf.high"], 2))`], p `{r} pvalr(wgs_results[[3, "p.value"]])`) while carrying a HOXB13 mutation increase risk by `{r} round(wgs_results[4, 2], 1)` times (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[4, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[4, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[4, "conf.high"], 2))`], p = `{r} pvalr(wgs_results[[4, "p.value"]])`). The interaction term was not significant (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[7, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[7, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[7, "conf.high"], 2))`], p = `{r} pvalr(wgs_results[[7, "p.value"]])`), therefore we have presented only the main effect model here. 

To compare the PHS and HOXB13 models directly, we calculated the PHS HR for a similar proportion of the population as are HOXB13 carriers. Since 1.7% of subjects carried a HOXB13 mutation, we calculated the HR between the top 1.7% of PHSes and the median PHS and found that someone in the top 1.7% of PHSes had a `{r} round(wgs_phs_95[[1, "value"]], 2)` times greater risk of PCa than the median individual (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs_95[[1, "value"]], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs_95[[1, "conf.low"]], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs_95[[1, "conf.high"]], 2))`]). By comparison, a HOXB13 carrier had a `{r} round(wgs_hoxb13[[1, "value"]], 2)` times greater risk of PCa than a non-carrier (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_hoxb13[[1, "value"]], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_hoxb13[[1, "conf.low"]], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_hoxb13[[1, "conf.high"]], 2))`]).

## Comparison of cohort incidence rate to the general Norwegian population from the cancer registry

To evaluate how generalizable our results were to the population of Norway, we compared the incidence rate in each cohort for both any PCa and for metastatic PCa to the predicted annualized incidence rate from the Norwegian cancer registry. Cancer registry data were for prostate cancer cases in Norway for the years 2014-2017 as reported by Huynh-le et al. (2020). First, we fit an exponential model to the average incidence for each 5-year age group. For any PCa, the best fit was an exponential quadratic and for metastatic PCa the best fit was a simple exponential. We then predicted the annualized incidence from this model and calculated the cumulative incidence rate from the cumulative sum of cases. We compared these to the cumulative incidence rates derived from the Cox PH model for each cohort and each phenotype (PCa or metastatic PCa). Given that the NFCS cohort was recruited based on a family history of cancer and that the incidence rate for this cohort displayed a systematically higher risk of PCa than the general population, we chose to focus on the HRs from the models fit to the HUSK data for the following analysis (@{suppfig-comp}).

## Predicting population risk of prostate cancer onset based on HR from the HUSK cohort

Finally, we looked at the predicted risk stratification for PCa in the general population based on the HRs from our PHS models.  Here, we used the exponential models fit to the data from Huynh-Le et al. (2020) as described in the previous section as the population baseline incidence rate. We then stratified these curves by the HR for the top 20% and bottom 20% of PHSes from the Cox PH model fit to the HUSK cohort data as reported in @{tbl-1}. We performed this separately for any PCa and for metastatic PCa (@{fig-strat}).

Based on an individual's age and PHS, we can see their instantaneous risk for developing PCa within the next year in @{fig-strat}A. For example, a healthy (i.e., cancer-free) individual at age 75 who is in the top 80% of PHSes has about a 1.5% risk compared to someone in the bottom 20% who has about a 0.75% risk. There is a considerably higher predicted incidence rate for individuals with PHS in the top quintile than the baseline with around 50% more cases in this quintile than in the baseline at age 75. It is important to note that the decline in incidence rate after 70 in @{fig-strat}A in is likely an artifact of reduced screening rather than a real decrease in incidence rate (cite Hunhy-Le 2020).

# Discussion

We observed strong stratification in both Norwegian cohorts, which demonstrates good performance of PHS601 in a population distinct from the development population. The strong stratification in the HUSK cohort demonstrates good risk stratification in the general population. In addition, the NFCS cohort was recruited based on self-reported family history of cancer and showed elevated cancer-risk relative to the general Norwegian population (@{suppfig-comp}). Given the strong risk stratification in this group, this suggests that genetics in this model is not just a proxy for family history.

For metastatic disease, we also saw good stratification between high and low risk individuals based on PHS. In the NFCS cohort, the effect was only marginally significant with the 99% confidence intervals for the HR barely overlapping 1.00. However, we see a similar magnitude effect with greater confidence in the HUSK cohort. This suggests PHS601 could be effective at identifying individuals at greater risk of metastatic disease and therefore with the greatest clinical benefit for further screening via PSA or imaging.

In addition to testing the general performance of PHS, we also wanted to compare PHS to screening for RPVs such as HOXB13. Even in the case of low sample sizes, for example, in the NFCS cohort we had only `{r} p212_sample_size[1, 3]` cases of prostatic cancer and `{r} p212_sample_size[2, 3]` cases of metastatic disease, the polygenic score was more useful than sequencing in the same sample size. In addition, genotyping for polygenic scoring costs a fraction of sequencing (source? numbers on this?). A much larger percentage of the population are affected by a high risk score than are affected by currently known PRVs. High polygenic risk affects 50x more people than BRCA2 mutations, which means genetic risk scoring is more useful for more people. If someone is a carrier of a pathogenic mutation in BRCA2 or HOXB13, that tells you they have a relatively high risk of developing cancer, however, it provides no information about the relative risk of patients without those rare variants. Whereas, a polygenic risk score can inform risk in all patients. Evaluating how this could work in Norway, there is more value per NOK for PHS screening than for sequencing. PHS has a potentially larger public health benefit.

The combined Cox model with both PHS and HOXB13 was also significant, which suggests that both polygenic score as well as rare deleterious mutations contribute independently to PCa risk. As we show, having a high PHS score does not appear to predict being a carrier of HOXB13 G84E. Therefore, both of these genetic factors can provide valuable information about individual risk. It is possible that clinical interventions differ between individuals whose phenotype arises from rare deleterious mutations and individuals whose phenotype arises from the interaction of environment with genotype of the normal array of segregating genes of minor effect. Furthermore, RPVs and PHSes have different implications for genetic counseling for example, for the risk of offspring being affected in the case of RPVs.

While the time varying effect of PHS was weak, we did see a significant negative trend in the HR of PHS with age in two independent cohorts such that the strongest effect of genetic risk was at the youngest ages (40s). This has a couple of implications. First, the genetic risk stratification appears to be the strongest at younger ages (at least with the portion of genetic variation captured by this model) and, in fact, would be stronger than the model suggests averaged across all ages. For example, in the HUSK cohort, the HR for any PCa was 1.54, whereas in the time transformed model the HR at age 40 was 1.87. From a utility perspective, this is valuable because we want to identify individuals at risk of early diagnosis who might benefit the most from modifying their risk through lifestyle interventions, pharmaceuticals, or early screening. Second, this suggests that the impact of genetics decreases with age such that congenital risk is greatest in younger individuals and that factors other than genetics, such as lifestyle, have a greater influence in older subjects. Future modeling efforts could investigate adding a time-varying component to PHS models to further improve risk stratification based on age and genetic risk.

Future Directions

One limitation of this study is the limited sample size of subjects with diagnosis data, age of diagnosis, and metastasis code. If we could get a bigger data set, we could potentially identify additional SNPs specific to the Norwegian population.

While information on metastatic or aggressive disease is often lacking in study populations and sample sizes for metastatic disease are relatively small resulting in decreased power, advances in electronic health records systems and biobanks could improve the sample sizes and information necessary to identify individuals with metastatic disease. Therefore, future studies should develop models that are specific to the development of metastatic or aggressive disease

The benefit of using PHS for screening is that a clinician can identify how likely a patient is to develop disease and how likely they are to develop agressive/metastatic/clinically significant disease. This should be determine before deciding whether to measure PSA.
